answer.evidence: The main body shows a large horizontal interior floor (rows 12-36) seen from above, with a back wall above it (rows 1-10, windows). Its front edge is a light line at rows 35-37 (peak at row 37, #bcbdc3), followed by darker eave shadow at rows 38-40. Below this is a 26-row south face (rows 38-63) with two windows, a door and a brick lintel. The collapsed right corner is transparent at rows 12-42 and turns into a rubble heap at rows 43-63. The rubble is a heap and does not need its own top surface. No isometric side face is drawn.

styleAnswer.evidence: The measured facts put the candidate level with the references. It has 11 visible tones per tile against 12 and 10, near-flat coverage of 5% against 0%, and only 5% neutral dark edge pixels, so its outlines carry a tint rather than being a near-black sticker line. By eye the grey concrete ramps through about 4 steps, with speckle and crack grain on the floor and front wall. The rubble ramp is shaded stone by stone, and small rust and debris accents break up the surface. The collapsed corner, interior floor and front face all read as separate forms by value. It has fewer total colours (32 against 66 and 185) and slightly fewer shading steps than the references. The wall faces are somewhat plainer than the tiled roofs and stone courses, but they do not form large flat fills. A careful artist would accept it next to the references.

styleAnswer.evidence: Measured facts put the candidate at 11 visible tones per tile against 12 and 10 for the references, with 5% near-flat coverage and only 5% neutral dark edge pixels. So the outline is tinted and the numbers are not shallow. By eye, the grey concrete floor and wall faces use roughly 4 lightness steps, where the references use 5-6 on roof tiles and stone. The rubble, rust and debris speckle add some texture, but the concrete surfaces are mostly smooth grey with few grain dots, and the front wall has little per-block shading. The candidate has only 32 distinct colours in total, against 185 and 66 for the references. It reads as slightly flatter and thinner than the Beodeul pieces. A careful artist would likely ask for more grain and shading depth on the walls and rubble before accepting it next to the references.

answer.evidence: The main body has a large top surface in rows 1-36: a lighter wall rim at rows 1-4, a rubble-strewn floor in rows 5-34, and a light front-edge line at rows 35-37 (the column scan shows #bcbdc3 at row 37). Darker shadow rows 38-40 follow it. Below is a south face of about 26 rows (rows 38-63) with two dark windows, a door and a lintel. The right corner has collapsed into a rubble heap seen from above (rows 43-63), which counts as visible contents. The silhouette is not a flat top-down slab or a front elevation.

styleAnswer.evidence: Measured facts are on par with the references: 11 visible tones per tile against 12 and 10, 5% near-flat coverage, and 5% neutral dark edge pixels, so the outlines are tinted rather than black. By eye, the grey concrete walls and floor show speckle, cracks and rubble clumps, with a few rust and orange accents, and the pieces are separated by value rather than a uniform black line. It is weaker than the references in a few ways. Each material ramp has only about 4 steps, against 5-6 for the roof tiles and stone. The concrete wall face is fairly uniform with little per-block shading. The rubble ramp is soft and lacks stone-by-stone shading. Only 32 distinct colours in total, against 185 and 66, means less variation and grain overall. Overall it is a competent, textured piece but a bit thinner than the Beodeul pieces, so a careful artist would likely see it as slightly lower in richness. When in doubt, fail.
